answers_by_date.answer: No, no migrants may obtain dual nationality by retaining their nationality of origin
answers_by_date.basis: In force: Constitution 1980 Art. 10 No. 4 (foreigners naturalise 'renunciando expresamente a su nacionalidad anterior', except nationals of a country that grants Chileans the same benefit by treaty) and DS 5142/1960 Art. 2 (as amended by DL 1432/1976: renunciation of the nationality of origin is a requirement for the carta). This is the same rule the starting answer describes (renunciation plus the Spain treaty exception), so it is coded 'No' the same way. No practice evidence found for this period.

answers_by_date.answer: No, no migrants may obtain dual nationality by retaining their nationality of origin
answers_by_date.basis: Same as 2000: constitutional and statutory renunciation requirements in force, with the treaty (Spain) exception. Ley 20.050 was published on 26 Aug 2005, after this date. No practice evidence found.

answers_by_date.answer: No, no migrants may obtain dual nationality by retaining their nationality of origin
answers_by_date.basis: From 26 Aug 2005 Ley 20.050 replaced Art. 10 No. 4 with 'Los extranjeros que obtuvieren carta de nacionalización en conformidad a la ley', dropping the constitutional renunciation clause. But DS 5142 Art. 2 kept 'Será requisito ... que el extranjero renuncie a su nacionalidad de origen', unchanged until 2022. So the starting answer's 'No' still has a statutory basis. No practice evidence found.

answers_by_date.answer: No, no migrants may obtain dual nationality by retaining their nationality of origin
answers_by_date.basis: Unchanged since 2005: DS 5142 Art. 2 still required renunciation. Ley 20.888 (D.O. 08.01.2016, after this date and before 2020) amended Art. 2 on permanent residence, children aged 14 and over and children of refugees, but left the renunciation sentence in place. No practice evidence found.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

events.instrument: Ley 20.050, Reforma constitucional que introduce diversas modificaciones a la Constitución Política de la República
events.what_changed: Before: naturalisation required express renunciation of the prior nationality, except for nationals of a country that grants Chileans the same benefit by treaty. After: the constitutional renunciation requirement is gone, and Chileans lose their nationality only by voluntary renunciation. This liberalises the constitutional basis but leaves the statutory requirement in DS 5142 untouched.

events.what_changed: Added the permanent-residence requirement, a route for children aged 14 and over, and naturalisation of refugees' minor children. The sentence requiring renunciation of the nationality of origin was kept. No change on dual nationality.
events.passage: Será requisito para la concesión de la carta de nacionalización que el extranjero renuncie a su nacionalidad DL 1432 1976ART 2°de origen, o a cualquier otra adquirida o que pudiere corresponderle.

answers.notes: Pre-2005 Art. 10 was read in the Georgetown PDBA consolidated copy (amended to about 2001), because LeyChile would not display the body of DS 1150/DL 3464. The Chile–Spain Convenio de Doble Nacionalidad (1958) was not opened; its existence rests on the starting answer's citation and the old Art. 10 No. 4 treaty exception. The DS 5142 renunciation requirement in force 2000–2020 comes from DL 1432 (1976). LeyChile's 'texto original' layer (1960) shows the older notarial-renunciation wording, and its annotations attribute the later wording to DL 1432 Art. 2.

answers.repealed_search: Searched the pre-2005 constitutional text and the DS 5142 version history (1960 original, 2016 intermediate version, 2022 current) for any dual-nationality protection that was later repealed. None was found. The only change between 2000 and 2020 (Ley 20.050) widened the constitutional room for dual nationality and did not narrow it.

sources_opened.title: Constitución de Chile (PDBA Georgetown, amended text)

answers.sourcing_note: Dating is strong. Ley 20.050 and the DS 5142 versions were read on LeyChile, and the pre-2005 Art. 10 in a secondary consolidated copy, because the official DS 1150 body would not render. The Spain treaty was not read, and no practice evidence on naturalisation and renunciation was found for any period.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The 'No' has a statutory basis: DS 5142 Art. 2 required renunciation throughout 2000–2020. Two points cut against it, though. (1) The Spain treaty exception that the coder notes makes 'Conditional, depending on the country of origin' arguably the more accurate option on every date. (2) From 26 Aug 2005 the Constitution no longer requires renunciation, and a renunciation filed before Chilean authorities generally does not end the foreign nationality, so in effect many naturalised migrants keep dual nationality.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, there is an opportunity to regularize after certain conditions are met
answers_by_date.basis: DL 1.094 and DS 597/1984 were in force (the same regime the starting answer rests on). Executive regularisation processes were used: the October 1998 'amnistía provisoria' gave two-year temporary visas to about 22,000 people, mostly Peruvians, without a work contract (El Desconcierto 2018, retrospective). The practice evidence is thin and second-hand.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, there is an opportunity to regularize after certain conditions are met
answers_by_date.basis: Same DL 1.094/DS 597 regime, with no amendment touching regularisation found between 2000 and 2005. No practice evidence found specific to around 2005; rated from the neighbouring periods.

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, there is an opportunity to regularize after certain conditions are met
answers_by_date.basis: Same regime. The extraordinary 'Proceso de Regularización' ran from 5 Nov 2007 to 5 Feb 2008 for those who entered by October 2007 and had no criminal record, and benefited about 47,000–50,000 people (Cooperativa 2007; El Desconcierto 2018).

answers_by_date.answer: Yes, there is an opportunity to regularize after certain conditions are met
answers_by_date.basis: Same regime. LeyChile shows DL 1.094's last amendment before repeal was Ley 20.507 (in force 8 Apr 2011, trafficking/smuggling), with no change to the regularisation framework found. No specific practice source read for around 2015. The next documented practice is the 2018 process (about 155,000 enrolled, over 110,000 visas granted by December 2018, but only 20.8% stamped).

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 and neither the right protection nor the implementation level of these protections has changed

answers.notes: The bodies of DL 1.094 Arts. 71, 81 and 91 could not be read: LeyChile renders only the index for this repealed norm, and the PDF copies could not be parsed. The iura.cl index shows only their opening words (Art. 81 'Los extranjeros que ingresaren al territorio nacional sin dar cump...'; Art. 91 'Corresponderá al Ministerio del Interior la ap...'; Art. 71 'Los extranjeros que continuaren residiendo en el país después de h...'). So the statutory basis is taken from the starting citation, and the citation should be checked against the text. The regularisation processes of 1998, 2007–08 and 2018 were executive measures, not statutory amendments. The practice sources are press reports about irregular migrants generally, not specifically about workers.

answers.sourcing_note: Weak. The DL 1.094 article texts and their versions could not be read: only the LeyChile version metadata showing Ley 20.507 as the last amendment (2011) was visible. Practice evidence is second-hand press. Nothing was found for around 2005 or 2015, and nothing specifically on migrant workers.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The articles cited (DL 1.094 Arts. 81 and 91) appear to be the control/expulsion rule and the Ministry-powers rule, not a regularisation right. Under DL 1.094, regularisation rested on applying for a visa after paying overstay fines and on discretionary executive amnesties, while clandestine entrants faced criminal sanctions. 'Yes' is defensible but rests on discretion, and the citation should be checked.

answers_by_date.basis: Constitution Art. 10 No. 1 (pre-2005 text) excluded children of foreigners in service of their government and children of 'extranjeros transeúntes', who could only opt for Chilean nationality. There was no guarantee for children who would otherwise be stateless, and no statelessness provision in DS 5142. The administrative practice then treated children of irregular migrants as 'transeúntes' (UNHCR 2018, retrospective).
Same text as 2000. Ley 20.050 (26 Aug 2005) later amended Art. 10 Nos. 2–4 but left the No. 1 transeúnte exception intact.

Art. 10 No. 1 unchanged, with no statelessness guarantee. Ley 20.430 (2010) on refugees provides no nationality guarantee (not read for this indicator). The restrictive 'transeúnte' interpretation was still applied to children of irregular migrants.

No change to the constitutional or statutory text. In 2014 the authorities changed the administrative interpretation of 'transeúnte' (UNHCR 2018), which is a practice shift and not a statutory guarantee. Chile acceded to the 1954 and 1961 statelessness conventions only in April 2018, after this date.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

events.what_changed: Amended Art. 10 Nos. 2, 3 and 4 (children of Chileans born abroad; naturalisation) and left No. 1, birthplace nationality with the transeúnte exception, untouched. No statelessness guarantee was added.

En 2014, las autoridades modificaron la interpretación

events.what_changed: Allowed refugees' minor children to naturalise once a parent naturalises, and children aged 14 and over with permanent residence to apply. These are facilitation routes, not a guarantee against statelessness.

answers.notes: Ley 21.325 Art. 173 (cited for 2023) could not be read, because the LeyChile page rendered only about 25,000 characters. It entered into force in February 2022 and does not bear on 2000–2020. No Corte Suprema transeúnte ruling was read in full. Those rulings (2014 onward, granting nationality to individual children of irregular parents) are practice evidence and state no general statelessness guarantee. Pre-2005 Art. 10 was read in the PDBA consolidated copy.

provisions.in_force: 1981-03-11 to today (text of No. 1 unchanged by Ley 20.050)

answers.repealed_search: Searched the pre-2005 Constitution (Art. 10), the Ley 20.050 amendments and the DS 5142 versions (1960, 2016) for any guarantee of nationality to stateless persons or to children who would otherwise be stateless that existed and was repealed between 2000 and 2020. None was found: the only routes were the transeúnte option, naturalisation and 'especial gracia' by law.
answers.sourcing_note: The constitutional text and amendments were read, the pre-2005 text from a secondary consolidated copy. The 2018 treaty accession is documented only through a UNHCR note; its promulgating decree and status in domestic law were not read.
answers.starting_answer_concern: After Chile's April 2018 accession to the 1961 Convention (Art. 1: grant nationality to persons born in the territory who would otherwise be stateless), the 2020 'No' depends on whether that treaty was promulgated and is directly applicable in Chilean law. This was not verified. If it is, the 2020 answer could be 'Yes'.
